title: Punctuation and commands
goal: Look up the stroke for any punctuation mark, symbol, capital, cursor move, editing key or shortcut, and what each does to the spacing around it.

blocks.x: How punctuation strokes work

`rules/reserved/punctuation.json`: **117 strokes**: 65 marks and symbols plus 52 glued fingerspelling letters (listed on [the fingerspelling page](#/ref/fingerspelling/fingerspelling-in-running-text)). `rules/reserved/commands.json`: **82 strokes** ([below](#/ref/punctuation/commands)). All are [reserved](#/ref/reserved-strokes): no word takes them.

**One stroke per mark and per command** ([how it is chosen](#/ref/reserved-strokes/what-it-guarantees)). A mark differing in spacing or capital code (`{.}` and `{^.^}`, `{^-^}` and `-`) is a different output with its own stroke. The **Dictionary text** column is what the stroke sends. `^` next to a mark attaches it.

Glued fingerspelled letters

The other 52 strokes in `punctuation.json` are the glued letters `A*` a, `A*P` A, and so on for the alphabet. List and first-up rule: [the fingerspelling page](#/ref/fingerspelling/fingerspelling-in-running-text).
Commands

82 strokes in `rules/reserved/commands.json`. The `STPH` movement family and the F-keys are Lapwing's strokes minus its number-key variants (lyk has no number key). Omitted: Lapwing's repeated-arrow chords (such as `STPH-RS`, Left twice), its commands that open Plover's own windows (keymux has no counterpart) and `{MODE:CAPS}`. No caps-lock: for a run of words in capitals, strike [[KPA*L]] before each word. 30 strokes (the cursor and selection family, Backspace, and the toggle, show and hide controls of the overlay, tape, keyboard and lookup) send on the first key up: see [Send on the first key up](#/ref/punctuation/send-on-the-first-key-up).

blocks.x: Send on the first key up

A stroke normally goes when its **last** key comes up. An entry carrying the marker `{:firstup}` goes when its **first** key comes up, and the keys still down **wait**: the next key pressed makes a new stroke with them. Hold most of a chord and tap one key repeatedly; each tap is a stroke. Releasing the held keys alone sends nothing.

**Exceptions: `{:firstup:except=KEYS}`.** `KEYS` is one stroke in steno notation (hyphen where an outline needs it). The listed keys are exempt: the stroke goes when the first key **not** in the list comes up. Lifting an exempt key first sends nothing and the chord stays open; the exempt key is still part of the stroke that goes. A chord whose keys are all exempt goes on its last key up. A list that is empty or does not parse as one stroke counts as plain `{:firstup}`. Use it where a base is held and other keys are tapped, so lifting the base early cannot send the stroke with the tapped keys still down: the cursor family exempts `STPH*` (`{:firstup:except=STPH*}{#Left}{^}`), the modifier chords the right-hand base `-FRPBLGTS`, the glued letters the star `*`. Plain `{:firstup}` stays where no held base is fixed: Backspace [[PW-FP]] and the overlay, tape, keyboard, lookup and outline controls (their held keys change from one stroke of a family to the next). The spelling is exact, lowercase, no spaces; the marker sits in front of the `{^}` and the command.

Example: hold `STPH` (left hand) and tap `-R` three times: [[STPH-R]] three times, Left, Left, Left. Still holding, tap `-P`: [[STPH-P]], Up. Add `*` and the same taps select ([[STPH*R]], Shift+Left). Rule for every entry below: hold all but one key of the stroke, tap the last. The cursor entries exempt the held base `STPH*`: lifting it first sends nothing. In an entry the marker sits **in front of** the command and the `{^}`, `{:firstup:except=STPH*}{#Left}{^}`, never after, so a reader that does not know the marker reads the rest the same way. The marker types nothing and changes no spacing.

blocks.x: **Selection criteria:** commands that are naturally repeated; the family shares the left-hand base `STPH`, so a held `STPH` is a cursor chord; held base plus all but one key, plus the tapped key, makes exactly the next stroke of the family. Adding keys changes the family in place: `STPH-R` to `STPH-RB` (word left) with `-B`, `STPH-R` to `STPH*R` (select) with `*`; both are first-up too. The controls follow the same idea: a toggle, show or hide is a state flipped repeatedly without lifting the hand, and the overlay controls share the base `PHRO*L` as the cursor family shares `STPH`. In their entries the marker comes first, then `{:transparent}`, then the command: `{:firstup}{:transparent}{:overlay:toggle}`. Keymux reads each marker wherever it stands; the order is a convention that keeps the command last.
**Left out on purpose:**

head: Entry
Why it does not carry the marker
rows: Everything that types text: words, briefs, phrases, suffixes
Early send would send a half-struck word, and a held key would join the next word.
Punctuation, capitals, glued letters, the retro commands (`{*?}`, `{*<}`, `{>}`)
They change spacing or capitalisation, or act on the previous words; repeating or early send is an error.
Return submits forms and chat boxes, Escape cancels: they need the deliberate send of a fully released stroke, and repeating is rarely wanted.

Wanted repeated, but both strokes sit inside the keys of dozens of common words (89 and 26 among the 5,000 most common: *taken*, *goodbye*, *girls*, *details*) and are struck mid-sentence. Backspace has the same exposure (14 and 32) but is held most often, so it carries the marker.
83 and 38 common words contain these keys (*girl*, *together*, *forward*); `TPW` is the F-key base, so holding it taps into F-keys. Browser history is a deliberate step, not a repeat.
F1 to F12 and the clipboard and Super shortcuts (`KHR*F`, `KPH*F` and the rest)
Each is its own chord with no shared base: nothing to hold and tap, nothing useful to repeat.
Engine commands run once, and `{:back}` is a single erase.
[[PHRO*TZ]] (clear the tape), [[PHRO*PLZ]] (free the engine from RAM)
Destructive or one-shot: clearing twice equals once, and unloading should be a fully released stroke, not the first key of a chord. Both stay on the last key up.

Opening an open lookup does nothing, so nothing to repeat; the stroke is the widest of the controls: 18 of the 5,000 most common words have a stroke containing it and 11 more start with such a stroke, against 2 to 5 for the toggles. [[PHR*UP]] flips the lookup with hold-and-tap.

blocks.x: **The trap.** Keys still down when a first-up stroke goes join the next stroke. Lift the whole hand between a cursor move and the next word; a lagging finger rides into the next stroke. A word whose stroke is a first-up stroke plus more keys is hit only if one of its keys lands after another has come up, which a chord struck together never does. Exposure among the 5,000 most common words: 3 for `STPH-R` and `STPH-RB` (*insurance*, *internal*), 15 to 19 for `STPH-P` `-B` `-G`, 0 to 6 for the rest of the family, 14 and 32 for Backspace. The controls, counted as words whose single stroke contains the control's keys plus longer words whose first stroke does: 3 for `PHRO*L`, 0 for `PHRO*LS` and `PHRO*LD`, 1 for `PHRO*T`, 5 for `PHRO*B` (*belong*, *belongs*, *belonged*, *unbelievable*, *balloon*), 4 for `PHR*UP`, 2 for `PHRUPD`; none is a word typed in a hurry.
What runs it

Keymux implements first-key-up sending: its translator flags entries carrying `{:firstup}` or `{:firstup:except=KEYS}`, and its engine sends the stroke when the first key (not in KEYS) comes up. The exception needs a keymux build that has it; an older build does not read it, so install that build before `lyk deploy`. `disable_first_up: true` in Keymux's config ignores the marker everywhere; every stroke then goes on the last key up. Dictionaries without the marker (e.g. plain Lapwing) are unaffected. Besides the command strokes, every modifier chord (`LGTS` ender) is first-up: hold the right-hand modifier keys and tap characters on the left, with the right-hand base exempt. So is every glued fingerspelling letter: hold `*` and tap letter chords, with `*` exempt.

**Plover does not know `{:firstup}` or `{:firstup:except=KEYS}`.** Plover reads `{:name}` as a call to a registered meta plugin; none is called `firstup`, and Plover 5.4.2 raises `KeyError: 'firstup'`. In plain Plover the 30 strokes above error instead of acting, as do the glued letters and modifier chords below; every other stroke is unaffected. The marker is harmless only in an engine that knows it. lyk deploys to Keymux, so the 30 strokes carry it; a Plover user can register a one-line no-op meta plugin named `firstup`, or use copies of `commands.json`, `punctuation.json` and the modifier dictionary with the marker removed. The strokes do not change either way. The 1,470 [modifier chords](#/ref/fingerspelling/modifier-chords-the-lgts-dictionary) carry the marker too (`{:firstup:except=-FRPBLGTS}{^}{#super(1)}{^}`), and the same holds for them; so do the 52 [glued letters](#/ref/fingerspelling/fingerspelling-in-running-text) (`{:firstup:except=*}{>}{&a}`).

Overlay and lookup controls (Keymux)

Strokes that show, hide and flip Keymux's overlay (keyboard diagram and tape) and live lookup; the two outline strokes are in [Outline notation](#/ref/punctuation/outline-notation-keymux). Each of these types nothing, keeps surrounding spacing and capitals, runs once and stays off the tape. **They act only on an already-running overlay, and only for the session:** nothing is written to the config, and they never start the overlay or change how it starts; a restart follows the config. With no overlay running (or `enabled: false`) they do nothing, with no error.

blocks.x: Use them to read off the outline of what you just wrote, or of a stroke before you commit to it. **Key layout.** Both keep the `PHRO*` control base and share `-PB` (N, notation); `-R` adds *recent* (what was just struck), `-T` adds *then* (the stroke that follows). They are not nested in each other, so no hold-and-tap from one lands on the other. Both are free of every word outline, backup and phrase, and of every start of a multi-stroke entry. Each carries `{:firstup}{:transparent}` like the toggles above; `{:transparent}` keeps surrounding spacing and capitals and keeps the stroke off the translation history. Needs a Keymux that knows `{:outline:last}` and `{:outline:next}`.
The transparent marker

A stroke carrying `{:transparent}` is invisible to the translation history. A lookup mid-join does not break it: `THAS`, [[PHRUP]], then `+EUFG` still joins as if the lookup had not been struck, and `*` after the lookup skips past it. Every control needs it. The marker sits **in front of** the command, like `{:firstup}`, types nothing and changes no spacing. Related Keymux markers no lyk stroke uses: `{:barrier}` (end any join here) and `{:nobarrier}`.
History helpers
Five more Keymux-only commands act on the typing history. None needs the overlay.

head: Stroke
Definition
Effect
rows: Put back what `*` took back (`{:redo:2}` for two)

Take back a whole word: a stem and the suffixes glued to it, and every stroke of a `+` run the solver read (`*` takes one stroke back at a time). Needs keymux `d5c96dc` or later; an older keymux takes back only the run's last stroke
Say the last thing once more

Erase the last character of what was typed, as part of the history: `*` types it again (`{:back:3}` erases three; no stroke). With nothing typed to erase it presses Backspace. [[PW-FP]] is the Backspace key itself, which `*` cannot bring back. `{:back}` is a barrier (see [the undo stroke](#/ref/punctuation/the-undo-stroke)): `*` takes the erase back first and goes no further back than it

blocks.x: The name lane's opener

`#` alone (number bar, nothing else down) is the entry `{}`: types nothing, changes nothing. It is a stroke keymux records: the solver reads it from keymux's stroke history and reads the run struck right after it as a name ([the name lane](#/ref/names)). A `#/...` name entry is a longer match and wins. `#` held with other keys is not this entry.
The undo stroke

The lone `*` (star key by itself) is the undo stroke: `*` is `{:undo_or:Control_L(BackSpace)}`. It takes back the last real stroke as Plover's `*` does (undone strokes can be put back with [[R*EUD]]; transparent strokes such as the overlay controls are skipped; a held `*` repeats one undo per repeat). At a **barrier** it differs: after an arrow, Home/End, Page Up/Down, Delete or Escape, a Backspace or Delete word operation, or any shortcut with Ctrl, Alt or Super, the text before the cursor move is no longer next to the cursor, so undoing would delete text elsewhere. There `*` does not undo: it sends **Ctrl+Backspace** (delete a word at the cursor), uses the barrier up and forgets what was before it. The next `*` is an ordinary undo of the strokes struck after the barrier. With nothing left to undo, `*` also sends Ctrl+Backspace. Keymux decides this (steno-layer setting `undo_stops_at_barrier`, on by default); lyk chooses the stroke and the fallback keys. **Needs Keymux commit 137459d or later.**

head: Stroke
Definition
Effect
rows: Undo the last real stroke; at a barrier, or with nothing to undo, Ctrl+Backspace

Plain undo, no fallback: at a barrier or with nothing to undo it does what Keymux's plain undo does there (with `undo_stops_at_barrier` on, Ctrl+Backspace once). Keeps the old behaviour of `*` under its own stroke

blocks.x: [[TK*UPS]] is the undo family beside [[TK*UP]] (undo a word): `-S` is the plain, single step. Keymux also accepts `{:undo_or:ctrl+backspace}` as an alias; lyk writes the canonical form. To change the fallback, edit the `"*"` line in `rules/reserved/commands.json` (e.g. `{:undo_or:Escape}` for undo-else-Escape).
A reader that does not know keymux's metas

**A dictionary reader that does not know keymux's metas** (plain Plover is one) reads `{:name}` as a call to a registered meta plugin and raises `KeyError` (as for `{:firstup}`) for `transparent`, `overlay`, `tape`, `keyboard`, `lookup`, `outline`, `engine`, `back`, `undo_or`, `redo`, `undo_word`, `again` and `swap`. In plain Plover those 20 strokes error instead of acting; every other stroke is unaffected. **`*` is the one that matters**, the most-used key: its `{:undo_or:...}` meta raises `KeyError`, so the lone `*` does not undo. Workarounds: a copy of `commands.json` with `"*": "=undo"` (Plover's own undo) and the other 19 entries removed; or no-op meta plugins with those names (fine for the overlay, which does not exist there; a no-op `undo_or` leaves `*` dead). The theory is unchanged; Keymux is the target engine.
